item.title: The Midterm Money Machine: Where Campaign Ad Dollars Are Flowing in the Final Weeks
item.body:
With Election Day on November 3 less than a month away, the last stretch of the 2026 midterm campaign is also its most expensive. Candidates, party committees and outside groups are all competing for a limited supply of airtime, inbox space and phone screens. Here is where the money tends to go in the closing weeks, and what those choices reveal about how each side reads the political map.

*Note: This article is a general explainer. Spending totals change daily, so check ad-tracking firms and the Federal Election Commission (FEC) for current figures.*

## Why the final weeks cost the most

Political advertising follows a predictable pattern. Spending ramps up as Election Day approaches, and the last few weeks are the most crowded. There are a few reasons:

- **Voters are paying attention.** Many people tune in only when early voting begins and ballots arrive in the mail.
- **Early voting compresses the calendar.** In many states, voting is already underway, so a message has to land before ballots are returned, not just before Election Day.
- **Rates rise with demand.** Broadcast stations sell time in a competitive market, and prices tend to climb when many campaigns want the same slots. Federal candidates get legal protections on the rates they pay, but outside groups often pay more.

## Where the dollars go

### Broadcast and cable television

Local broadcast TV is still the largest single line item in most competitive races. It reaches older, high-turnout voters efficiently, and those voters make up a large share of midterm electorates. Costs are highest in expensive media markets, and a statewide race in a large state can require buying time in several of them.

### Streaming and connected TV

Connected TV, which includes ads served on streaming services and smart-TV platforms, has become a fast-growing part of campaign budgets. Its main appeal is targeting. A campaign can aim at a specific geography or audience instead of paying for every viewer in a market. Streaming does not replace broadcast, but many strategists now treat it as a complement, especially for reaching viewers who rarely watch live television.

### Digital and social

Online display, search, video and social ads serve several purposes. Some are persuasion messages. Others raise money, recruit volunteers or remind supporters how and where to vote. Major platforms set their own rules for political ads, including disclosure requirements and, in some cases, restrictions in the final days before an election, so campaigns plan their digital calendars carefully.

### Text, mail and direct outreach

Texting, direct mail and phone outreach are less visible than TV but central to turnout efforts. In the closing weeks, they are used to provide polling-place information, promote early voting and urge supporters to return mail ballots. Campaigns must comply with federal and state rules on messaging and consent, and responsible operations build those compliance steps into their programs.

## Which races absorb the most money

Ad money is not spread evenly. It concentrates in a small number of contests that are close enough for spending to plausibly change the outcome.

- **Competitive U.S. Senate races.** Statewide contests in battleground states draw the most spending because they cover multiple media markets and can decide control of the chamber.
- **Governor's races.** Open seats and tight contests in large states can produce enormous ad budgets.
- **Key U.S. House districts.** Control of the House typically turns on a few dozen competitive seats. Party committees and affiliated super PACs often spend heavily in those districts, particularly in expensive markets such as the New York and Los Angeles areas, where TV costs are high.
- **Ballot measures.** In some states, referendums and initiatives on issues such as taxes, abortion access or election rules attract eight-figure campaigns of their own.

## What the spending says about the map

Strategists often say that where a group puts its money is the clearest signal of what it believes. Reading the spending patterns can offer a few clues.

**Defense versus offense.** When a party or allied group books time in a district it usually wins, it is typically playing defense and worried about erosion there. Money in territory the other side holds suggests confidence that the seat is within reach. Shifts from week to week, such as a group canceling reservations in one race and adding them in another, are closely watched as a sign of internal polling.

**Expanding or shrinking the battlefield.** Late reservations in a race that was not on the radar months ago suggest the map is widening. Pulled reservations may mean a campaign has concluded a race is either safe or out of reach.

**The role of outside groups.** Super PACs and other outside organizations can raise large sums and often fill gaps that candidate committees cannot, particularly because candidates and parties have contribution limits that outside groups do not. Some of these groups disclose donors; others, such as certain nonprofits, have more limited disclosure. That is one reason transparency advocates keep a close eye on the final-month filings.

**Candidate fundraising strength.** In some races, one candidate has a clear fundraising advantage. In others, the candidate who is behind on money is helped by party or outside spending that narrows the gap on the air.

## What viewers and voters should know

- **Check the disclaimer.** Federal ads must state who paid for them. "Paid for by..." and "I approve this message" lines show whether an ad came from a candidate, a party committee or an outside group.
- **Look up the sponsor.** The FEC database and state election offices publish campaign finance reports, and independent trackers publish ad-spending data.
- **Remember that an ad is advocacy.** Campaign ads are designed to persuade. Claims about opponents are often selective, and fact-checking organizations and nonpartisan voter guides can help provide context.
- **Make a plan to vote.** Rules on early voting, mail ballots and registration deadlines vary by state. Your state or local election office is the most reliable source for dates and locations.

## The bottom line

The late-campaign surge in political advertising is a reminder that elections are shaped by both messages and logistics. Which markets get ads, which screens are targeted and which races attract outside money all reflect each side's view of where the next majority will be won or lost. By Election Day, the spending map will say a lot about what campaigns believed was in play, even before the votes are counted.
